item.title: Top House Dem sparks backlash with plan for deported Dreamers that goes beyond bringing them back
item.description: Hakeem Jeffries says he would support bringing deported DACA recipients back to the U.S. and providing remedial assistance to those treated unfairly.
item.content:encoded:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said Tuesday he supports bringing deported DACA recipients back to the U.S. and providing what he called "remedial assistance," prompting critics to accuse him of wanting to pay deported immigrants.

Jeffries replied "certainly" when asked during a PBS NewsHour interview whether he would support bringing deported DACA recipients back to the U.S. He also said those he believes were treated unfairly by the Trump administration should receive "remedial assistance."

"Anyone, whether they are a citizen, whether they were here lawfully, whether they're DACA recipients, who've been treated unfairly and unjustly by the administration, we need to provide remedial assistance to them and undo the damage that's been done to the country, to law-abiding immigrant families and to the American people over this last 20 months or so," Jeffries told PBS News.

JEFFRIES VOWS DEMOCRATS WON’T ‘GIVE A DIME’ TO TRUMP’S DEPORTATION EFFORTS

DACA offers eligible immigrants brought to the country illegally as children temporary protection from deportation and the ability to apply for work authorization, but does not grant legal immigration status, according to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services.

Jeffries did not specify whether the "remedial assistance" he proposed would include financial compensation. His office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment on Wednesday.

Podcaster Benny Johnson similarly criticized Jeffries in a social media post on Wednesday, alleging that Democrats "always put foreigners before Americans."

"Hakeem Jeffries says he wants to re-import DACA recipients that have already been deported and pay them," Johnson said. "This is the future under Democrat control. They will always put foreigners before Americans."

"DISGUSTING: Incoming House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY) supports bringing back DEPORTED DACA recipients and providing them with money and assistance to 'undo the damage that’s been done to the country,'" conservative account Red Wave Press added on X.

"Hakeem Jeffries wants to bring back deported DACA recipients and pay them. Under far-left control, American citizens will always come second and be expected to pay for it. Every. Single. Time," another X user posted.

"EVERY TIME Dems want any form of amnesty, it's to make them voters, and use those voters to open the floodgate, then get citizenship to millions more," Eric Daugherty, chief content officer of Florida’s Voice, claimed Wednesday in an X post responding to Jeffries' remarks.

Jeffries also claimed during the interview that the U.S. currently has a "broken immigration system" that "needs to be fixed."

BORDER DEM POISED TO WIELD ICE PURSE STRINGS REJECTS SOCIALIST ‘DEFUND’ PUSH

"Well, certainly, on the immigration front, we have a broken immigration system. It needs to be fixed," Jeffries said. "It should be fixed in a comprehensive way."

"Immigration enforcement should be fair, just and humane," the New York Democrat added. "We're not going to provide a dime to the administration's violent mass deportation machine. Let's work together, perhaps beginning with moving the Dream and Promise Act this Congress as a foundation for the type of work that can be done in the next Congress."

DHS CHIEF FIRES BACK AT JAYAPAL OVER CLAIM MAJORITY OF IMMIGRATION ARRESTS POSE 'NO THREAT'

Jeffries’ comments come after Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Monday raised the possibility of Congress creating a pathway to permanent legal status for DACA recipients.

HOUSE REPUBLICANS MOVE TO MAKE TRUMP'S BORDER POLICIES PERMANENT

"If we want to have an immigration reform to where we can look at DACA and figure out a way that these individuals can become maybe legal permanent citizens or something like this, that’ll be up to Congress," Mullin said.

DHS did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment.

TRUMP REAFFIRMS ICE ARREST POLICY AFTER CONFUSING GUIDANCE SPARKS ALARM AMONG AGENTS

DHS emphasized in a March 3, 2026 X post that DACA "does not confer any form of legal status" in the U.S.

"To be clear: DACA does not confer any form of legal status in this country," DHS said in the social media post. "Any illegal alien who is a DACA recipient may be subject to arrest and deportation for a number of reasons, including if they’ve committed a crime."

"Between January 20, 2025, and September 28, 2025, ICE arrested 264 DACA recipients nationwide — and MORE than 92% were illegal aliens charged or CONVICTED of a crime in the U.S.," the post continues.

The White House on Monday left open the possibility of working with Democrats on an immigration deal for illegal immigrants who have lived in the U.S. for more than a decade without committing other crimes, though Trump and Mullin both ruled out amnesty.

item.title: Angel Reese and Caitlin Clark became racial symbols, but their responses tell different stories
item.description: Angel Reese has embraced representing Black women since LSU's 2023 title, while Caitlin Clark has pushed back against racial framing of their rivalry.
item.content:encoded:
As Angel Reese and the Atlanta Dream faced Golden State in the WNBA Finals, some of the coverage made it sound as if they were representing Black America.

An Oct. 24 Swish Appeal column connected Atlanta’s enthusiasm for the Dream to the city’s history of "Black excellence, resistance and pride." It quoted a historian who linked the team to Martin Luther King Jr.’s vision of the "Beloved Community."

ANGEL REESE’S WNBA FINALS SHOWED HOW CRITICISM OF HER PLAY BECOMES AN ACCUSATION OF RACISM

There’s nothing wrong with a city seeing its history and culture reflected in its sports teams. The Pittsburgh Steelers’ name and logo celebrate the steel industry that helped define their city. It’s perfectly reasonable for Atlanta fans to find a similar connection between the Dream and their own community.

The problem arises when supporting a player becomes a test of racial loyalty, or criticizing her becomes an attack on the people she supposedly represents.

I encountered plenty of that while covering Angel Reese during the Finals. People who disagreed with my questions and columns decided the explanation was that I had a problem with Black women. Somehow, evaluating one basketball player had become a statement about millions of people I wasn’t writing about.

But this fits a much larger pattern involving Reese and Caitlin Clark. For some fans and commentators, they have become stand-ins for Black America and White America. Their successes and shortcomings get recruited into arguments about privilege, discrimination and whose achievements deserve recognition.

But Clark and Reese have responded very differently to those roles.

When pressed, Clark has pushed back against people using her name to promote racial agendas but has repeatedly emphasized that basketball is her job.

In the closing moments of LSU’s 2023 national championship victory over Iowa, Angel Reese followed Caitlin Clark around the court, repeatedly taunting Iowa's star player. She made the "you can’t see me" gesture, then pointed to her ring finger.

Many people, myself included, took issue with Reese's taunts. Predictably, commentators, including ESPN’s Stephen A. Smith, framed the backlash as a racial double standard, pointing to Clark’s use of the same gesture earlier in the tournament.

Of course, there's a clear difference between doing a gesture toward your own bench and following an opponent around the court and doing it in her face, but the nuance was lost on many.

Even one of the Louisville players, Hailey Van Lith, later explained that Clark’s gesture was directed at Iowa’s strength coach, not anyone on the Cardinals team.

But Reese had already made it about race herself, right there at the postgame podium.

After a reporter asked Reese about the outrage on Twitter surrounding her celebration, Reese claimed she was labeled as "too hood" and "too ghetto." She continued by saying the victory was for "the girls that look like me" and declared, "It was bigger than me tonight."

Imagine Clark saying a championship was for "girls that look like me." I don’t believe the same commentators defending Reese would applaud that message from Clark.

In an August 2025 Forbes interview about her signature shoe, Reese described being "a visual and a voice for young Black women." Discussing people who shared her experiences, she added, "I’m speaking for those people, young girls, young boys."

Reese has also made it clear that she wants to be known for more than basketball.

"It’s always been both: basketball and fashion," she told Vogue in 2025. She's also made appearances at the Met Gala in each of the past three years.

Good for her. She’s built a following and figured out how to make money from it. There’s nothing wrong with that, and it doesn’t mean she doesn’t care about winning.

But Reese has spent years talking about race and positioning herself as a voice for Black women. So when some of her defenders treat criticism of her as an attack on all Black women, they aren’t making that connection entirely on their own.

During a July game against Atlanta, Toronto coach Sandy Brondello complained to officials after a foul call involving Reese and Nyara Sabally. The broadcast picked up Brondello describing Reese as a "protected species."

Brondello is Australian. As Australia’s ABC explained, that expression is commonly used in Australian sports to complain about players receiving favorable treatment from officials. It had nothing to do with Reese's race.

WHY ISN'T ANGEL REESE HELD TO THE CAITLIN CLARK STANDARD WHEN FANS ATTACK HER TEAMMATES?

Brondello apologized anyway and explained that her frustration was with the officiating. The WNBA suspended her for one game, and Reese accepted the apology, thanked the league for acting and said there was "no place for discrimination or hate."

Reese then went further: "I speak for a community that believes in the bigger picture of things."

Brondello was arguing about a foul call, but Reese used the moment to talk about discrimination. Once again, the racial framing was coming from Reese herself.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Clark has been pulled into these arguments, too.

In June 2024, she was asked about people using her name in broader cultural debates. "Basketball is my job," she said, explaining that she couldn’t control what others said online.

Even that answer became a controversy. WNBA player DiJonai Carrington claimed people were using Clark’s name to justify bigotry and accused Clark of not being bothered by it.

"Silence is a luxury," Carrington wrote.

Later that day, asked specifically about racism and misogyny, Clark said, "People should not be using my name to push those agendas."

In both instances, it was the WNBA media prodding Clark to make a statement about racial animosity, not something Clark brought up on her own. Instead, Clark tried to keep her focus on basketball. Of course, that didn't satisfy the media or WNBA players demanding that Clark answer for online trolls.

See, that's the bigger issue here. There's an expectation that Clark must be accountable for people she neither controls nor authorizes to speak for her. The same principle applies to Reese; neither player is responsible for policing every account that claims to support her.

In her December 2024 TIME interview, Clark said, "I want to say I’ve earned every single thing, but as a white person, there is privilege."

I believe Clark felt pressured to make that statement after all the grief she’d taken for trying to keep the focus on basketball. When staying out of the argument gets you criticized, there’s pressure to give people the statement they’ve been demanding.

And it didn’t end with her rookie season. As I recently documented, the demands have continued through all three of Clark’s WNBA seasons.

During a podcast appearance in July 2025, Nancy Armour acknowledged that Clark had already addressed the subject, including in her TIME interview. But Armour wanted a stronger statement, delivered on Clark’s own initiative instead of in response to a question.

USA TODAY WRITER INVOKES EMMETT TILL, SAYS CAITLIN CLARK PUTS BLACK AND QUEER PLAYERS 'IN DANGER' BY FLOPPING

In October 2026, podcaster Charlotte Wilder said that despite Clark addressing online trolls multiple times, Clark needed to say "something a little more forceful."

Then, at her October 2026 season-ending news conference, Clark was asked about Kelsey Mitchell’s comments on the treatment she receives as a Fever player. Clark again rejected people using her name to promote racism, hate or discrimination.

Three seasons into her WNBA career, Clark is still being asked to explain that she doesn’t support racism. How many more statements are required?

Reese helped Atlanta reach the Finals, and she deserves credit for that. But she also deserves criticism for her poor performances over the final four games. Treating her as an individual leaves room for both.

The same goes for Clark. Her performances and public comments are fair game. But some troll calling himself a fan doesn’t make her responsible for whatever he posts online. And the media doesn’t get to assign her that job.

The players themselves have also complicated the idea that they are permanent personal enemies.

During September’s FIBA Women’s Basketball World Cup, Reese also spoke positively about playing alongside Clark and developing their chemistry as USA teammates.

After they won gold together, Clark was asked whether she and Reese were friends now.

"We’ve always been friends," she responded. "Don’t try to do that."

They can compete against each other, talk trash and still function perfectly well on the same team. And fans don’t have to like them equally.

What I reject is the demand to choose a racial allegiance along with a favorite player.

Admiring Clark’s game doesn’t make someone hostile to Black women. Supporting Reese doesn’t require someone to dismiss every legitimate criticism of her. Their accomplishments belong to them, and so do their mistakes.

Neither gets to stand in for an entire race, and neither should be forced to.

Root for whoever you want. Just stop making it a racial loyalty test.

item.title: Chris Harrison’s ‘The Vow’ sparks ‘trad wife’ debate among contestants as emotions run high
item.description: Chris Harrison's faith-based dating show "The Vow" follows Jace Cates as he meets 10 women seeking traditional marriage on a Texas Hill Country property.
item.content:encoded:
WARNING: Spoilers from this week's episodes of "The Vow" below.

Chris Harrison is challenging modern dating culture with a reality series focused on faith and commitment.

The former "Bachelor" host returned to reality television Wednesday with the two-episode premiere of "Chris Harrison's The Vow" on Fox Nation, introducing viewers to a new approach to finding love centered on Christianity and traditional values.

The first two episodes, "And So It Begins..." and "Beauty is Fleeting," followed Jace Cates, a 30-year-old mortgage loan officer from Oregon, as he met 10 women hoping to become his wife. But what began with prayers and promising first impressions quickly turned emotional as two contestants were sent home.

'THE VOW' BRINGS CHRIS HARRISON BACK TO REALITY DATING TV: WHAT TO KNOW ABOUT THE FOX NATION SERIES

"There will be no roses, no elimination ceremonies, no gimmicks to distract from real life," Harrison explained during the premiere.

Harrison said the series was created in response to a dating culture increasingly shaped by swiping, hookups and fleeting relationships.

"Connections got faster, easier, but a lot less meaningful," he said. "What happened to the kind of love that lasts?"

Before meeting the women, Jace opened up about his own heartbreak, explaining that he had previously been engaged before realizing something was missing from the relationship.

"When my engagement ended, it was extremely hard," he said. "It was absolutely my lowest point."

Jace said his faith helped him navigate the breakup and ultimately recognize what he wanted in a future wife.

"Dating's not a game for me, I'm doing it because I want to meet my wife and start our life together," he said.

As the 10 women arrived at the Texas Hill Country property, conversations quickly turned to traditional marriage, motherhood and what it means to be a wife.

Alexis Wyborny challenged the stereotype that traditional wives must spend their days in the kitchen.

Watch: Women debate what it means to be a 'trad wife' on Chris Harrison's new dating show

"A lot of people think about a traditional marriage or they're calling a trad wife right now as somebody who wears a muumuu and makes sourdough bread all day, every day," she said.

Alexis described herself as an independent woman who earns her own money, while Kierstin Zankl expressed interest in eventually becoming a stay-at-home mother.

Sierra Wood, meanwhile, spoke openly about her decision to remain a virgin until marriage.

"I'm wanting to save myself till I'm married," she said.

Another contestant, Mya Draper, made her intentions clear, saying she hoped to become a wife and mother.

"I would love to just be a mom and be a wife and do my husband for a living and have a big family," she said.

When Jace finally entered the house, he opened the evening with a group prayer before Harrison surprised everyone with their first challenge: preparing the property for the night.

Instead of a traditional cocktail party, the women worked alongside Jace to arrange furniture, prepare food and set up the outdoor space.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

The evening produced several promising connections, including one with Sierra, who discovered that she and Jace lived approximately 20 minutes apart in Oregon and attended the same church.

However, the night took an unexpected turn when Jace pulled Kierstin aside and ultimately sent her home, leaving nine women competing for his heart.

In the second episode, "Beauty is Fleeting," Jace's search for a wife continued as he selected Mya for the season's first one-on-one date, a horseback riding adventure through the Texas countryside.

During their time together, Jace discussed his broken prior engagement, while Mya shared the heartbreaking loss of her father in a car accident two years earlier.

Jace praised her vulnerability, and the two shared a kiss.

"I haven't allowed myself to fall for someone in so long, but I'm definitely falling for Jace," Mya said afterward. 

The romance continued during a group basketball outing, where Jace introduced the women to his former college coach and spent time playing with children.

"I'm excited to see how the women interact with the kids because I want that family so bad," he explained.

But the outing also sparked tension when Jace selected Marley Alexander for a romantic dinner overlooking Austin, leaving several contestants feeling overlooked.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Jace and Marley's dinner exposed major differences in their expectations for marriage.

Marley, who had been single for seven years, explained that she wanted to travel before having children and preferred to remain close to her family in Texas.

Jace, however, said he was ready to settle down and start a family much sooner.

"Our timelines couldn't really be further apart and that's not a knock on Marley. That's just reality," he said.

Despite their initial attraction, Jace decided their differences were too significant to overlook and sent her home.

Marley accepted his decision, telling Jace she trusted God's timing.

With Kierstin and Marley eliminated, eight women remain as Jace continues his search for a wife.

The first two episodes of "Chris Harrison's The Vow" are now streaming on Fox Nation, with new episodes dropping every Wednesday.

item.title: Ancient burial site packed with treasures plus 38 bodies discovered after centuries
item.description: A 600-year-old burial complex at Chan Chan, Peru, contained 38 bodies, metal headdresses and ceremonial objects, including one skeleton whose unusual position puzzled experts.
item.content:encoded:
Archaeologists in Peru have uncovered a 600-year-old burial complex holding 38 bodies — including one skeleton whose unusual position has raised questions about the possibility of human sacrifice.

The graves were discovered at Chan Chan, an ancient pre-Incan city near Trujillo, Peru, roughly 350 miles north of Lima.

Peru's Ministry of Culture announced the discovery earlier this fall, saying the nearly intact Chimú burial site had remained hidden for over six centuries.

COLOSSAL TOMB TIED TO ALEXANDER THE GREAT REVEALED BY OFFICIALS: 'UNIQUE AND MAGNIFICENT'

Images shared with Fox News Digital by officials at the Ministry of Culture show an assortment of ancient ceramic vessels, including decorated jugs and pottery with sculpted figures.

Other photos offer an overhead view of the burial complex, revealing its network of chambers, walls and stairways.

The burial complex contained three chambers, including a central chamber holding one individual surrounded by artifacts made from shell and metal, according to the Ministry of Culture.

One side chamber contained weapons and metal emblems, while another held 20 bodies. Archaeologists found 18 additional individuals elsewhere in the complex, bringing the total to 38.

7,000-YEAR-OLD BONES UNCOVERED AT CONSTRUCTION SITE IN STARTLING FIND

One skeleton stood out because it was buried fully extended, unlike typical Chimú burials, in which bodies were placed in bent or seated positions.

"This unusual characteristic raises new questions about the circumstances surrounding the individual's death and has led researchers to consider several hypotheses, including the possibility of a sacrificial ritual or an extreme difference in social status compared with the other individuals buried in the same space," the ministry said in a statement translated from Spanish.

The burial goods included metal headdresses, earrings, necklaces, carved wooden boxes and ceremonial objects made from seashells and quartz.

Some of the buried individuals also had red pigment on their heads, which officials said was "used exclusively in high-ranking burials in Andean societies."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Officials added that the fragile remains must be carefully documented before they can be removed from the site.

"Because the skeletal and organic remains are extremely fragile after centuries of deterioration caused by time and coastal humidity, scientific protocols require that no evidence be removed without first conducting a thorough examination and documentation of its original context," the statement said.

Researchers will first take hundreds of photographs to create a detailed 3D model of the burial site before carefully removing the remains and artifacts by hand.

Jorge Meneses, an archaeologist with Peru's Ministry of Culture, said in a statement that the discovery offers a rare opportunity to study ancient Chimú burials that have remained largely undisturbed.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

"What was known about elite Chimú tombs before this discovery came from funerary platforms that had been looted and destroyed since colonial times, with disturbed and incomplete archaeological contexts and valuable objects displayed in collections and museums," Meneses said.

"Now, archaeologists have the opportunity to study the individuals and artifacts exactly as they were placed inside this platform nearly 600 years ago," he added.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The Ministry of Culture plans to publish its full findings in a forthcoming book, offering further insight into the ancient Chimú civilization and its burial practices.

Peru, a country rich in ancient history, has yielded numerous archaeological discoveries in recent years.

Last summer, utility workers digging a natural gas line in Lima, Peru, discovered a well-preserved, 1,000-year-old female mummy buried just 20 inches below the surface.

In August 2025, utility workers digging trenches for a natural gas project in Lima, Peru, uncovered two 1,000-year-old tombs in a single day.

item.title: LUKE BALL: The midterm warning signs for Democrats no one is talking about
item.description: Democrats swept House and Senate races, but conservative ballot initiatives on voter ID, DEI and gender policies passed in the same blue states.
item.content:encoded:
Democrats have been deliriously giddy since the midterm elections.

Their party, rudderless and defeated for two years, appeared to come roaring back into relevance with a House and Senate majority. The once-defunct political careers of establishment Democrats like Chuck Schumer roared back to life, as even traditionally safe Republican seats faced the wrath of a disgruntled electorate.

But as Democrats celebrated their candidates’ wins in campaign offices across the country, dozens of conservative victories went largely unnoticed in the very same states Democrats claimed were now solidly blue.

ELAINE PARKER: DEMOCRAT WIN IS A WAKE-UP CALL FOR REPUBLICANS, NOT A VOTE FOR SOCIALISM

The Democrats’ victories were a backlash against broken Republican promises. They were not a mandate to usher in a vast liberal policy platform.

To understand this argument, you must look past the boisterous celebrations from the left’s election night parties and look a little further down the ballot. Across the country, voters codified conservative policy priorities through ballot initiatives that liberal groups spent millions of dollars to fight against. And even more surprisingly, those historically conservative initiatives found success in states that flipped blue on election night.

Let’s look at just a handful:

On election night, Colorado elected a Democratic senator, a Democratic governor, and is on track to have only one Republican out of eight seats in the state’s entire congressional delegation. You would think that means any conservative ballot initiative would have gone down in flames.

But that’s not what happened.

Colorado voters delivered a stunning rebuke to some of the left’s most entrenched policy platforms. Proposition 134, written to keep men out of women’s sports, passed decisively. Proposition 135, banning gender transition surgeries on children under 18, passed as well.

The same phenomenon happened in other so-called blue states.

North Carolina passed a ballot initiative to require voter ID on mail-in ballots by almost the same percentage with which it elected a Democrat senator. Even left-leaning statewide outlets in the Tar Heel state are calling on Democrats to pump the brakes on their midterm celebrations, pointing out the large number of unaffiliated voters in the state could cause true problems for Democrats in just a few short months.

DEM FLIPS KEY SENATE SEAT IN BATTLEGROUND NORTH CAROLINA AS COOPER DEFEATS TRUMP ALLY

Arizona Democrats swept in the state’s legislative and gubernatorial elections, but failed to stop a Republican-led ballot initiative designating cartels as terrorist organizations. Despite fierce opposition from Democrats in the Arizona legislature, it passed Tuesday by over 13 points. The liberal bastion of Washington state voted in favor of biological sex requirements for school sports while electing Democrats. Nevada passed voter ID requirements while electing a Democratic governor and members of Congress. Wisconsin elected a Democratic governor on the same ballot where they soundly rejected far-left progressive DEI policies.

JAMES CARVILLE CAUTIONS DEMOCRATS TO STAY AWAY FROM DEI POLICIES AFTER MIDTERM VICTORIES

In short, Democrats might need to pack away the party hats.

The midterm down-ballot election results present Democrats with a conundrum: How are they to successfully govern when the ideological positions their party has championed for years were so firmly rebuked by their own constituencies? Do they press forward with wildly unpopular policies and ignore the mandate from voters, or do they evolve and adapt to the will of the people?

There is yet another hurdle Democrats face as they prepare to assume House and Senate majorities in January: a large portion of the midterm electorate that propelled them to victory was comprised of independents and swing voters. That coalition is at odds with the base of the modern Democratic Party.

For the last three years, the Democrats’ base has been largely energized by Democratic socialist candidates and policy proposals. One in three Democrats now identify as Democratic socialists themselves. How are Democrats going to find long-term favor with their diverse midterm electorate of independents and swing voters who do not identify with socialist policies?

JONATHAN TURLEY: MIDTERMS EMPOWER DEMOCRATS TO TARGET THE ELECTORAL COLLEGE

If the more moderate Democrats in party leadership try and maintain the coalition of independents and swing voters, they will upset their party’s progressives. If the moderates try and appease the progressives, they will lose the independents and swing voters.

It’s a lose-lose situation.

Ultimately, I believe we will watch the Democrats self-destruct in spectacular fashion over the next two years as they fail to maintain their midterm coalition.

Moderates will cave — again — to the far-left progressives in their party. It’s what they’ve been doing for years. "Centrist" Democrats have put up all the resistance of a screen door in a hurricane to the rise of socialism in their party. As I noted in a recent appearance on "The Faulkner Focus," establishment Democrats may have been willing to allow the Democratic socialists into their "big tent party," but the Democratic socialists had no intention of allowing the centrists to remain with them in that tent.

For the next two years, centrists and far-left progressives will fail to play nicely with one another. They will not advance substantive legislation; they will be fixated on investigations and impeachments.

Democrats will be their own worst enemy. They will do themselves no favors as they try and force their unpopular agenda, once again, on an electorate who already rebuked it at the ballot box. Republicans must seize the opportunity to recapture this crucial coalition of independents that propelled Donald Trump to victory in 2024.

Voters roared against the GOP’s broken promises by electing Democrats across the country. But it’s the down-ballot whispers that will help us chart the road to victory in 2028.

item.title: Seattle mayor backs effort to block girls' sports initiative that passed in 36 of Washington's 39 counties
item.description: Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson backs the Seattle School Board's legal action against Initiative 638, the transgender sports measure voters passed by 13 points.
item.content:encoded:
The statement was 148 words. Not one of those words was "girls."

Tuesday, Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson said that she was going to back the Seattle School Board's unanimous vote to pursue legal action against Initiative 638 — which would enforce separation of boys and girls in K-12 sports in Washington state. 

Voters passed the measure by a 13-point margin last week, and it won in 36 of the Evergreen State's 39 counties. But after deliberating behind closed doors Monday, the Seattle School Board voted publicly to authorize potential legal action against the measure without hearing public testimony. And the mayor fully approves.

Here is Wilson's full statement.

DEMOCRATS ACCUSED OF 'NO KINGS' HYPOCRISY OVER PUSH TO CHANGE VOTER-APPROVED TRANS SPORTS MEASURES

"Last night, the Seattle Public Schools Board of Directors voted to authorize legal action regarding Initiative 638. The Board's decision reflects concerns shared by educators, families, community leaders, and the City of Seattle about the measure's impact on student privacy, safety, dignity, and equitable access to educational opportunities.

"For nearly two decades, Washington schools and the Washington Interscholastic Activities Association have relied on policies designed to ensure all students can participate fully in school life. As those longstanding protections face new challenges, we affirm the rights of transgender youth and stand with them and their families.

"As mayor, I remain committed to building a Seattle where every person is welcomed, supported, and valued, and where all young people can thrive as their authentic selves. I support the Board's decision and its commitment to creating inclusive learning environments where every student has the opportunity to reach their full potential."

WASHINGTON STATE VOTERS APPEAR TO PASS FIRST-EVER BALLOT MEASURE SEPARATING BOYS AND GIRLS SPORTS

Remember, Seattle was one of the epicenters of the "No Kings" movement, where tens of thousands rallied against a president they accused of disregarding the will of the people. Yet when Washington voters overwhelmingly supported a measure Wilson opposes, she had no problem backing an effort to overturn it. Apparently, the will of the people is only worth defending when the people vote the right way.

Capping off Wilson's statement was a paragraph of political platitudes so empty it would make even a seasoned politician blush. She wants to build a Seattle "where all young people can thrive as their authentic selves," and "create inclusive learning environments where every student has the opportunity to reach their full potential."

This sounds great to an untrained ear, but what Wilson is really saying is this: If you're a boy who wants to identify as a girl, you should have the right to dominate females in sports. The dozen or so girls' cross-country runners from Camas, who walked off the start line to protest their male teammate competing as a female? They don't matter. Battle Ground High cross country runner Elise Bierer, who broke down in tears after sacrificing a race for the same cause? Irrelevant. Tumwater High student Frances Staudt, who is regularly cursed at by classmates for refusing to compete against a boy in a basketball game? Collateral damage.

Speaking of Staudt, she was at a political watch party in Redmond, last week with women's sports advocate Amy Sousa. Both were ecstatic about the passage of I-638 and thought this fight was over. But Monday, Sousa said she confronted the Seattle School Board, told them the vast majority of counties in Washington voted "yes" on I-638 and yelled, "King County doesn't get a veto!"

I followed up with her on that on Wednesday.

ACLU OF WASHINGTON SAYS IT WILL SUE TO BLOCK BALLOT INITIATIVE TO PROTECT GIRLS' SPORTS

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

"Those girls (like Staudt) have fought so, so hard," Sousa said. "They should not have to be activists at that age. And they should not be thrown into a political issue that adults put on their doorstep. Adults did this to them, and adults need to stop it."

As for what the legal fight looks like? Well, Monday, a group of parents and education organizations, represented by attorneys from the ACLU of Washington, Legal Voice and Pacifica Law Group, filed a lawsuit seeking to block I-638 before it takes effect Dec. 3. The plaintiffs argue that the measure's sex-verification requirements violate Washington's constitutional protections for privacy and equal rights. They're seeking an emergency injunction to prevent the initiative from taking effect while the case proceeds.

That's separate from the Seattle School Board authorizing its own potential legal action, though district officials have yet to specify what form that might take.

What's certain is that Seattle's mayor will be behind those actions. She's all about inclusion.

Except when it comes to the vast majority of the state's voters. Like anyone who may have wanted to testify in front of the school board, they are summarily excluded.

item.title: NFL and all its teams honored memory of military service members on Veterans Day without any fumbles
item.description: All 32 NFL teams honored Veterans Day on social media, a stark contrast to the handful of clubs that skipped Merry Christmas greetings in 2025.
item.content:encoded:

America's most popular sports league long ago tied itself to the United States military through various programs, with color guard presentations during the national anthem, and impressive stadium flyovers, so it was no surprise Veterans Day was recognized by the league and all of its teams.

All of them.

THREE NFL TEAMS ROASTED FOR CELEBRATING INDIGENOUS PEOPLES' DAY ON COLUMBUS DAY, WHICH NO TEAM EVEN MENTIONED

JUNETEENTH WAS CELEBRATED ACROSS MAJOR PROFESSIONAL SPORTS LEAGUES AND TEAMS — WITH TWO NOTABLE EXCEPTIONS

THE NFL IS AMERICA'S MOST GOD-CENTERED PROFESSIONAL SPORTS LEAGUE AND SUNDAY'S GAMES CONTINUED TO PROVE IT

item.title: GOP governor and prominent Dems congratulate senator-elect on flipping Mississippi seat blue
item.description: Prominent Democratic political figures and Mississippi's GOP Gov. Tate Reeves congratulated Scott Colom for winning the state's U.S. Senate race.
item.content:encoded:
Mississippi's Republican Gov. Tate Reeves, former President Bill Clinton and former Vice President Kamala Harris were among those to congratulate Democrat Sen.-elect Scott Colom on his victory in the Magnolia State's U.S. Senate contest.

More than a week after Election Day, The Associated Press on Wednesday called the race for Colom, the district attorney for Mississippi Circuit Court District 16, defeating President Donald Trump-backed incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.

"We may have had to count One Mississippi, Two Mississippi, but Blue Mississippi sure has a nice ring to it! Scott, you put your heart and soul into this race because you believe in the promise of your state’s people. And they believed in you right back. I’m honored to have stood alongside you. Congratulations!" Clinton said in a Wednesday post on X.

DEMS PROJECTED TO SCORE HISTORIC UPSET IN DEEP-RED MISSISSIPPI, TOPPLE TRUMP ALLY HYDE-SMITH

Colom is the first Democrat to win election to a Mississippi U.S. Senate seat since 1982; the late Sen. John Stennis, who served in the U.S. Senate from late 1947 until early 1989, was the last Democrat to serve as a U.S. Senator in the state.

"Congratulations to Senator-Elect @scott_colom. I hope to collaborate as we continue our very important work to support Mississippi families, grow jobs and wages for our people, and improve educational outcomes for our kids!" Gov. Reeves wrote in a post on X.

Colom shared the governor's post and wrote, "Thank you for the congratulations @tatereeves. I also look forward to working with you on the issues that matter to our state. Together, there’s nothing our beautiful state can’t accomplish." He added the hashtag, "#MississippiMatters."

KAMALA HARRIS URGES DEMS TO 'BE RUTHLESS' WITH POWER AFTER MIDTERMS, DEMANDS TRUMP ACCOUNTABILITY

Colom will be the third Black person ever to serve as a U.S. senator in Mississippi, the state's first Black senator since the 1800s and the first Black person popularly elected to serve as a senator from the state, since the prior two men were selected by the state legislature prior to the adoption of the 17th Amendment in the 20th century.

"The power is with the people, and the people of Mississippi are with Scott. @scott_colom makes history today as the first Black senator elected in Mississippi since Reconstruction. I saw firsthand when campaigning with him in his hometown that he is a brilliant leader and dedicated public servant who will work tirelessly to serve every Mississippian with pride. Congratulations, Scott," Harris wrote in a post on X.

SOROS NETWORK TARGETS DEEP-RED MISSISSIPPI IN BID TO FLIP SENATE SEAT

Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., said in a post, "Congratulations to Scott Colom on winning his election and making history as Mississippi's first Black senator since Reconstruction. Scott ran on a bold agenda — taking on Big Tech, the billionaire class and corruption in Washington — and WON. Scott: Welcome to the Senate."

item.title: NYC building collapse: Fifth body recovered as first responders search for survivors
item.description: FDNY crews are continuing rescue operations in Brooklyn's Flatbush neighborhood after a three-story building collapsed Wednesday, leaving an unknown number of people trapped.
item.content:encoded:
Three more bodies have been recovered from the rubble of a three-story building that collapsed in New York City on Wednesday afternoon, bringing the death toll to five, city officials said.

When the building in the Flatbush neighborhood of Brooklyn initially came down, the New York Fire Department reported two deaths. An unknown number of people remain trapped inside, officials said.

The collapse left 19 people injured, including a firefighter. Four were taken to area hospitals in critical condition, while the others sustained minor or non-life-threatening injuries. Over 12 hours later, the rescue operation is ongoing with over 250 fire and EMS personnel on the scene.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said the FDNY received a 911 call reporting the collapse at 1321 Flatbush Avenue at 4:01 p.m., with firefighters arriving within one minute and immediately launching efforts to find people in the rubble.

MANHATTAN HIGH-RISE EVACUATED AS OFFICIALS WARN OF POTENTIAL COLLAPSE

Rescue crews are deploying drones to survey the wreckage from above and vacuum trucks to safely remove debris as they search for anyone who may still be buried.

The city's Department of Buildings (DOB), which has inspectors and engineers on the scene, has launched an investigation into how the collapse happened. A cause has not been determined.

The building, which had a store at street level and apartments upstairs, fell into an open construction site next door at 2625 Bedford Avenue.

The developers at 2625 Bedford Avenue had active permits for excavation and foundation work in order to construct a new building, which is set to be three stories tall. 

In March, the city's Department of Buildings (DOB) issued a stop work order after inspectors found that the developers had demolished the existing building on the site without providing adequate shielding to neighboring properties, including 1321 Flatbush Avenue.

Just over a month later, DOB investigators found out that the demolition had continued in violation of the stop work order, which resulted in the contractor being fined $10,000, per city records. 

By May, the stop work order was lifted after the developers came into compliance, according to the DOB.

The DOB said Wednesday's collapse at 1321 Flatbush Avenue prompted officials to once again halt all work at 2625 Bedford Avenue.

item.title: Dems admit uncomfortable election sweep truth as party descends on Denver to shape 2028 without a frontrunner
item.description: Pete Buttigieg, Josh Shapiro and other 2028 presidential hopefuls gather in Denver to debate the Democratic Party's direction after midterm wins.
item.content:encoded:
DENVER — Fresh off sweeping midterm victories, Democratic leaders, strategists and potential 2028 presidential contenders are heading to Colorado to debate what comes next for their party.

The three-day "What’s Next" conference in Denver, organized by the independent group Majority Democrats, will bring together a broad slate of leaders from within the party as an advisor for the group admitting to Fox News Digital that the election results do not prove "validation of our party," but is more a "repudiation of Donald Trump."

The conference organizers hope to bring together Democrats to see "where our party goes from here."

The lineup includes former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, who ran in the Democratic presidential primary in 2020; Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro; Sens. Cory Booker, D-N.J., Raphael Warnock, D-Ga., and Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich.; Sen.-elect James Talarico, D-Texas; New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill; Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger; Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif.; and former Obama advisor David Axelrod.

KAMALA HARRIS URGES DEMS TO 'BE RUTHLESS' WITH POWER AFTER MIDTERMS, DEMANDS TRUMP ACCOUNTABILITY

Democrats, as they prepare to take control of Congress in January, are seeking to capitalize on their electoral gains and strategize on how to make good on the campaign promises that won them control of both chambers of Congress and many usually red state Houses — like affordability and healthcare. Organizers describe the gathering as a chance to assess the 2026 results and discuss the leaders, ideas and debates that could shape the party through 2028 and beyond.

The conference was scheduled even before Democrats' sweeping midterm victories earlier this month, when they saw historic seat flips not just in traditional Republican strongholds like Texas, Kansas and South Carolina.

Democrats must now turn those midterm gains into a governing agenda that reaches beyond their energized base.

Party leaders have pledged to lower costs, improve government services and investigate the Trump administration, but the party still faces questions about how to unite its progressive and moderate wings.

VOTERS PUNISHED THE GOP OVER COSTS; NOW, DEMOCRATS FACE THE AFFORDABILITY TEST

The conference is not an official Democratic Party event. Hosted by Majority Democrats, a group led by Rep. Jake Auchincloss, D-Mass., it is billed as an "independent, outsider conversation" about the party’s future.

Lis Smith, a longtime Democratic strategist and veteran of several presidential campaigns, serves as a senior adviser to the group and said the post-midterm election event would take an honest look at the party’s recent victories and what comes next now that they will control the House and the Senate.

"Democrats won big last week, but let’s be honest: the election was more a repudiation of Donald Trump than a validation of our party," Smith told Fox News Digital. "That’s why Majority Democrats is bringing together some of the biggest names and brightest new voices in Democratic politics at ‘What’s Next’ to have honest conversations about what worked, what didn’t and where our party goes from here."

"This is a once-in-a-generation opportunity to redefine what it means to be a Democrat, and our party can’t afford to squander it," she added.

The conference’s high-profile guest list could also offer an early glimpse of the party’s 2028 presidential field, fueling speculation about who may seek the nomination.

With no clear frontrunner, the gathering gives potential contenders a chance to share their views as Democrats consider who might lead the party’s next campaign. For now, their more immediate test will be delivering on the promises that helped them win the midterm elections.

item.title: Viral olive oil shots could lead to weight gain, health expert warns
item.description: Celebrities and social media users swear by daily olive oil and lemon juice shots, but a science consultant warns of weight gain and other health risks.
item.content:encoded:
Taking shots of olive oil has become a popular trend on social media, with celebrities like Kourtney Kardashian and Hailey Bieber touting the practice for its supposed health benefits.

However, some health professionals disagree with the claim that shooting olive oil is a viable wellness ritual.

"I think health trends like these become popular because they're novel and go viral," Megan Meyer, Ph.D., a science communication consultant based in Durham, North Carolina, told Fox News Digital.

BLOOD SUGAR SPIKES COULD HINGE ON THE ORDER YOU EAT YOUR FOOD, STUDY SUGGESTS

"I also think people are interested in quick, convenient health fixes. Improving your diet can often be challenging and take a good bit of time and the effects of an improved diet usually take even longer."

Reality television personality Harry Jowsey took to social media to share his experience taking olive oil and lemon juice shots every morning for a week straight, saying the main difference appeared in his face, with "less puffiness" and "more even skin."

Another social media user posted about a similar experience, calling the practice "a great way to lower inflammation."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Polyphenols are consistently mentioned by those praising olive oil for its nutritional qualities.

Produced by plants, polyphenols can help combat oxidative stress and reduce inflammation, which can lead to a variety of health benefits, according to the National Institutes of Health.

"One important caveat: polyphenol content in olive oil can vary quite a bit," Meyer said. "Extra virgin olive oil tends to have more polyphenol content than a light-tasting olive oil that has been refined."

When included in a healthy diet, olive oil can support heart health.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

An observational study published in 2022 in the Journal of the American College of Cardiology (JACC) found that adults who consumed more than half a tablespoon of olive oil per day had a 19% lower risk of death from heart disease.

"The heart health benefits are largely tied to the monounsaturated fat and polyphenols of olive oil," Meyer noted.

Taking a shot of olive oil "should be safe for most healthy people," according to Meyer.

However, she added, those with gallbladder issues, chronic reflux or a sensitive stomach should probably avoid it.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Weight gain is a real possibility, too.

"Taking an olive oil shot or two every day can add several hundred calories to your daily calorie consumption," Meyer said. "Consuming more calories than your body burns each day leads to weight gain, so taking an olive oil shot or two daily will most likely lead to weight gain over time."

"In addition, consuming that much fat on an empty stomach may lead to an upset stomach, acid reflux, bloating or loose stools," she noted.

Ultimately, Meyer does not recommend taking olive oil as a shot, but she supports consuming it in other forms.

"Olive oil is delicious," she said. "Instead, I recommend enjoying olive oil as part of your meals — as an oil for sautéing foods, as a base in dressings or finish with a drizzle on soups and sauces."

item.title: Senate Republicans fear 'brutal' 2028 map could keep Dems in power for years to come
item.description: Bernie Moreno called the 2028 Senate map "absolutely brutal" for the GOP as Republicans face defending deep-red seats in both Carolinas and Iowa.
item.content:encoded:
The aftershocks of last week's midterm elections are still being felt by Senate Republicans, but another political reality is beginning to set in: The GOP may not regain control of the chamber for years to come.

This year’s Senate map was, initially, favorable to Republicans in their quest to maintain and possibly grow their 53-seat majority in the Senate. But the next election cycle’s map in 2028 is tough, perhaps even insurmountable, for Republicans to conquer.

The Senate GOP’s newly minted campaign chief, Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, acknowledged that the map to reclaim the majority in 2028 is "very tough."

Democrats only have three incumbents up for re-election in battleground states, while Republicans have to defend seats in a slew of once-safe, deep-red states, including both Carolinas, Kansas and Iowa, among several others.

His home state, which just turned a shade of purple with Sen.-elect Sherrod Brown’s victory over Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, is in play again, too.

Moreno, when asked to sketch a 30,000-foot view of what the future fight for power would look like, told Fox News Digital that Republicans had "dealt with tough situations before."

"Look, it is an absolutely brutal map, but, politics, things change pretty quickly," Moreno said. "So we'll see how it is, but we're gonna be extraordinarily disciplined, we're gonna be extremely honest with our data. We [will] make certain that we hold our incumbents and our candidates accountable, and we're gonna make an appeal to donors as to how we should win."

SENATE GOP REBELS MOVE TO DELAY LEADERSHIP VOTE, DEMAND RECKONING AFTER MIDTERM DISASTER

Others were less optimistic.

Sen. Steve Daines, R-Mont., who chaired the National Republican Senatorial Committee during the 2024 campaign, when Republicans flipped the Senate, compared the situation to getting down early in a baseball game: Republicans would have to "chip away" at Democrats’ lead, but it would take time.

"Now the Democrats can't help themselves, but they'll overreach in the next couple of years," Daines told Fox News Digital. "They'll be out of step with where America is, and they'll provide an opportunity for us to win some Senate seats. But I think this will take a few cycles before we'll probably get back to the majority if I have to honestly interject and look at it."

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., who had just secured his position as the incoming minority leader after weathering a marathon venting session from Senate Republicans who are disgruntled and frustrated after the midterms, agreed that Democrats could overreach and create a "different shooting match" for Republicans.

SENATE GOP REBELLION FIZZLES AS THUNE KEEPS POWER DESPITE HISTORIC MIDTERM MASSACRE

But history has a way of repeating itself.

Thune shared the anecdote of how when he first arrived in the Senate in 2005, Republicans had clinched a 55-seat majority — "the high watermark for Republicans in the Senate, historically," he told Fox News Digital.

"We were very bullish about getting to 60 for the first time and having a filibuster-proof majority for the first time ever for Republicans in the Senate in 2006," Thune said. "And by 2006, we were back in the minority."

"The map matters for sure, but the mood of the country also really matters," he continued. "And there are a number of races this next cycle that have historically elected Republicans. Now there's Democrats sitting in those seats now, but every cycle is a little bit different, and as we saw this time around, the mood was moving against us."

The blowout losses across the map for Republicans do open up an opportunity for the next two years: running for their states and themselves, not for Trump, given that his time in office is winding down.

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., whose home state flipped after his decision to retire last year, and who has become a vocal critic of the administration, argued that 2028 was likely out of reach for Republicans and said the environment wouldn’t be ripe again until "at least 2030."

When asked if during the meeting that led to the eventual re-election of Thune as leader there was any reflection on the impact that Trump and his administration’s unpopularity with voters had, Tillis said, "I think there's probably a growing awareness of what I warned folks about in April of last year."

"And it wasn't really having that feedback loop," Tillis told Fox News Digital. "And I think we'll probably see a much healthier, more productive, more beneficial to the president feedback loop, where these people realize their performance is going to be what's going to be the driving force behind their re-elect."

"That's for the ones here," he continued. "And absent that, you know, I don't see any pickups. So I think everybody has to be realistic."

item.title: Young voters are not buying socialism. They want a made-in-America future
item.description: The Republican Party faces a young voter crisis as 73% backed Democrats in midterms, driven by housing costs and doubts about the American Dream.
item.content:encoded:
Young voters sent warning after warning to a Republican Party that remained tone-deaf, and one came wrapped in foil. When a Turning Point USA student complained that a burrito should not cost $20, some conservatives shifted the blame by lecturing young Americans to cook at home, eat ramen, find roommates and work additional jobs. "Burrito-gate" produced plenty of online jokes, but the frustration was never merely about lunch. It was about whether hard work still produces a better life.

President Trump brought voters under 30 close to an even split in 2024 and won a majority of young men, proving that this generation was willing to move right. However, the midterm election proved they were just as willing to move left toward the party they believed offered a more affordable future. A Fox News Voter Poll found that voters under 30 supported Democratic House candidates by 73% to 25%.

Young voters shifted left even as the broader electorate continued to favor capitalism over socialism. The same national poll found that 57% viewed capitalism favorably, while only 33% viewed socialism favorably. However, 69% believed the economy favors the wealthy. This shows the Republican hurdle: Americans believe in capitalism but doubt that today’s economy allows everyone to participate in the American Dream. A recent Harvard Youth Poll found that only 20% of young Americans said the democratic socialist label would make them more likely to support a candidate, while 31% said it would make them less likely and 45% said the label made no difference. Economic frustration gave Democrats an opening, but it did not turn an entire generation into blanket socialists.

BURRITO DEBATE RIPS OPEN GOP CIVIL WAR ON AFFORDABILITY: ‘WE WILL LOSE, AND DESERVE IT’

The Republican Party of family, faith and freedom tells young men to "man up," work hard, marry, become fathers and provide for their families. Young women are expected to "do it all" by working, building careers, marrying and becoming mothers. Building a Made-in-America life requires all young adults to afford bills, groceries and rent instead of living paycheck to paycheck. If they cannot afford housing of their own, guess where they are living? They are living with parents who are absorbing the affordability gap. The Federal Reserve found that 47% of adults ages 18–29 received outside help paying an expense, while 49% of adults under 30 lived with a parent, up 12 percentage points since 2019. Republicans cannot tell young men to man up or promise young women a future of homeownership, marriage and children while their parents are forced to finance the gap between a paycheck and independence.

I'M GEN Z: IF THE GOP WANTS MY VOTE, STOP THE SPEECHES AND FIX THE HOUSING CRISIS

Republicans must answer this frustration with a competence revolution that builds more attainable housing, removes barriers to ownership and turns a paycheck into independence. The strongest defense of capitalism is to build a nation of owners. Right now, young voters experience the economy through rent, debt and bills, not through ownership of their first home. Republicans should measure success results that families can see: faster permit approvals, more starter homes and rent or mortgage.

The revolution begins with housing. Currently, local fees, slow permitting, outdated zoning and land-use restrictions and barriers to manufactured housing limit supply and increase construction costs. Every Democratic proposal should face a litmus test: Does it produce more homes or just more government handouts to compete over the same limited supply? Scarcity only benefits investors by keeping more Americans renting longer, while existing homeowners gain equity as restricted supply drives property values higher. Local governments collect development fees, and large developers easily absorb delays that drive smaller builders out. Ultimately, every added fee and delay lands on the bill of first-time homebuyers.

TRUMP ACCOUNTS ARE JUST THE BEGINNING. YOUNG AMERICANS NEED A PATH TO HOMEOWNERSHIP

President Trump provided a blueprint for restoring the American Dream of homeownership through executive order by directing federal agencies to reduce regulatory barriers and create best practices for states and localities, including caps on permitting timelines and fees. 

He expanded that affordability agenda by directing the creation of a pilot program to proactively cancel mortgage-insurance premiums after qualifying homeowners build sufficient equity, lower refinancing costs and promote lower-cost factory-built housing. Republicans must accelerate these reforms and require officials receiving federal housing dollars to report permit times, construction fees and the number of homes produced in real time. The American Dream should be measured by homes built, costs reduced and more first-time buyers becoming homeowners.

Capitalism wins when a paycheck becomes savings and those savings become a down payment on a home. Republicans can tell young men to man up and young women to do it all, but they must build an economy in which stepping up still leads to a home, a family and a future. That is how Republicans defeat socialism: Make the American Dream affordable again.

item.title: Ro Khanna rejects warnings that Trump admin investigations could derail Democrats' affordability agenda
item.description: Ro Khanna says Democrats can pursue Trump investigations and tackle affordability at once, arguing accountability for the Iran war would lower prices.
item.content:encoded:
Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., is brushing off concerns that House Democrats’ eagerness to investigate Trump administration officials could distract the incoming majority from addressing Americans’ concerns about affordability.

"I can walk and chew gum at the same time," Khanna told Fox News when asked if the investigations could be a distraction.

Democratic lawmakers have repeatedly called to open probes into different allies of President Donald Trump after winning majorities in both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections.

BERNIE SANDERS WARNS DEMOCRATS NOT TO SPEND ALL THEIR TIME INVESTIGATING TRUMP

Khanna argued that Democrats using their oversight authority to subpoena Trump administration officials and others in his orbit won’t distract from the party’s ability to address affordability issues.

"We've got to have accountability, and then we also have to increase the minimum wage," Khanna said.

Khanna has been an advocate for impeaching Trump for a third time, saying it would be "setting a standard" of accountability. On NBC’s "Meet the Press," Khanna said that impeaching Trump would show that an administration cannot take action in Iran like he claims Trump has "without constitutional approval."

KAMALA HARRIS BREAKS WITH LEFT FLANK, WARNS DEMS THAT IMPEACHING TRUMP IS 'NOT A GOOD IDEA'

He told Fox News Digital that conducting investigations to hold Trump and his administration accountable, particularly for the war in Iran, could help lower food and gas prices.

"We've gotta end the war in Iran," Khanna said. "That's the biggest thing. We need accountability to end this war, and that would lower food and gas prices."

item.title: PATRICK K O’DONNELL: The untold story of America’s female Revolutionary sniper
item.description: Benedict Arnold's grueling 350-mile march to Quebec nearly destroyed his force, but Jemima Warner pressed on alone bearing her husband's rifle.
item.content:encoded:
Jemima Warner followed her husband into war. She didn’t know she’d take his place when he fell.

Jemima’s husband, James Warner, was an original member of the Continental Army and served in the 1st Pennsylvania Rifle Regiment. These crack-shot riflemen were among the best marksmen in Washington’s army. Many had been longhunters who lived and hunted beyond the Allegheny Mountains and often had to battle Native Americans. Their woodcraft, scouting skills and expert marksmanship helped pioneer many aspects of early American special operations. In the fall of 1775, Col. Benedict Arnold tapped them to help move his army through the Maine wilderness to attack Quebec.

Handsome, athletic and no more than 25 years old, James Warner was accompanied by his beautiful 17-year-old bride on the ill-fated journey. She was among a small group of women in the force known as camp followers. Two such women marched with the Pennsylvanians.

The full story of these remarkable riflemen and the role of the Pennsylvania long rifle in helping win the Revolutionary War can be found in my newest bestselling book, "Revolutionary Snipers: Washington’s Frontier Commandos Whose Marksmanship Forged a New Way of War and Helped Win the Revolution," the third book in a trilogy on the elite units of the war.

This groundbreaking look at the Revolutionary War recounts the untold story of the Continental Army’s first soldiers in an immersive "Band of Brothers"-style narrative that puts the reader in the boots of these snipers, who preceded today’s U.S. Army special operators. The book is also the first time the full story of Jemima Warner has been told.

AMERICA HAS FOUNDING FATHERS. A CATHOLIC SAINT WAS A FOUNDING MOTHER

In general, camp followers, known as "Mollies," had a complicated relationship with the military hierarchy. Many officers despised having these wives, mothers, daughters, mistresses and their children along, believing that they distracted the soldiers, slowed their movements and consumed food that could have fed the men.

Others were more pragmatic, noting that the men might not keep fighting if they couldn’t bring their wives. Washington wrote that he "was obliged to give Provisions to the extra Women in these regiments, or lose by Desertion, perhaps to the enemy, some of the oldest and best Soldiers in the Service."

EXPERTS FINALLY SOLVE MYSTERY OF TEENAGE REVOLUTIONARY WAR SOLDIER 246 YEARS AFTER HIS DEATH

Camp followers also provided valuable services to the Continental Army. Many worked as laundresses, earning rations and small fees for their labor. Others cooked or served as nurses. A few even spied on British camps while working as cooks or laundresses.

But the intrepid Jemima found herself doing more.

SECRETS OF REVOLUTIONARY WAR BATTLEFIELDS EMERGE 250 YEARS AFTER AMERICA'S FOUNDING

She had already marched hundreds of tortuous miles with the company when she found her husband at the foot of a tree, refusing to move, telling her he was "determined to die."

The 350-mile march from New England to Canada had become a grueling journey marked by starvation, torture and despair. The battle against the elements — freezing rain; swamps; bogs; snow; whitewater; traversing rivers, ponds and lakes with small, poorly crafted rafts and little to no provisions; drinking contaminated water — had proved deadlier than the British or the Native Americans. Many of the starving, exhausted men found themselves in the same situation as James, but without a wife to urge them on.

Jemima managed to press James forward for a few days "until he again sat down." Finding that all her solicitations could not induce him to rise, she had no choice but to leave him. In a final gesture of sacrificial love, the starving woman "placed all the bread in her possession between his legs with a canteen of water." She then took up his beloved rifle and resumed the march alone into the wilderness.

When Arnold’s beleaguered force eventually made it to Canada and, together with reinforcements, besieged the city of Quebec, the men were utterly shocked to see Jemima. "The widow of poor James Warner came to our quarters … bearing her husband’s rifle, his powder horn and pouch." She tearfully recounted the tragic story.

GEORGE WASHINGTON'S REMARKABLE PRAYER FOR AMERICA STILL RESONATES 250 YEARS LATER

The Americans had earlier sent an officer and an enlisted man bearing a white flag of truce into the besieged city of Quebec to offer American terms for surrender. The British had angrily responded by firing upon them with their artillery.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

So, when the American force demanded Quebec’s surrender for the second time in December 1775, instead of sending their troops under a flag of truce, they sent the intrepid Jemima Warner, fresh from her solo journey through the Maine wilderness, to deliver the message. Crossing no-man’s-land, the same ground where the previous party received enemy fire, Jemima entered the city and delivered the missive. The commander of the Crown forces burned the letter in front of her.

Fortunately, she returned alive. Courageous to the end, Jemima remained on the front lines. But on Dec. 11, 1775, Jemima Warner was struck and killed by British grapeshot during the siege, making her one of the first documented American women killed in action.

item.title: Trump faces a brutal impeachment era and needs a lawyer as press secretary
item.description: What President Trump and his advisers learned from the first impeachment circus of the next two years is valuable. There are major lessons that can be applied to the next two years.
item.content:encoded:
Impeachment proceedings for President Trump and Secretary of War Pete Hegseth are coming in the next two years.

That inevitability means President Trump would be well served by a superb young communicator who is a very smart lawyer as his next press secretary, especially if that person has demonstrated the extraordinary legal chops to have "Supreme Court clerk" on his or her résumé.

The duels with the White House press corps triggered by Trump-hunting in Congress, like those ahead with congressional committees, are very often going to deal with the extent of presidential powers. There is a lot of case law on that topic, and history is full of relevant precedents. A press secretary who knows those cases and precedents will be far ahead of the average journalist in the press room. If the new press secretary has to be briefed on Justice Robert Jackson’s famed opinion in the 1952 decision Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer, he or she will already be behind. President Trump cannot afford a spokesperson who is behind from the jump.

What President Trump and his advisers learned from the first impeachment circus of the next two years is valuable. The effort to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth this week was led by outgoing Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky. (Massie was booted out of his job of a dozen years in a May Republican primary, which Massie lost to Republican Ed Gallrein by nearly 10% — a stunning rebuke of Massie’s inveterate grandstanding.)

DEMOCRATS RALLY BEHIND GOP LAWMAKER'S HEGSETH IMPEACHMENT PUSH, SIGNAL MORE TO COME IN JANUARY

Massie failed in his last act in Congress, but the attention he attracted in failing demonstrated again that an attention-starved congressman can always get some cameras on him or her via moves to impeach anyone, anytime. Democrats noticed, especially achievement-free members like Massie who want some attention.

The foolishness of the latest impeachment push was demonstrated by its target, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, in a Tuesday morning press conference. Hegseth set an example of how to play offense against ridiculous charges: Speak in clear, crisp and detailed sentences. Reject in bold colors the antics of attention addicts. Then go back to work. Don’t get pulled into the weeds.

Massie is an attention addict, and he’s been contemplating the awful process of sudden withdrawal from his source of fleeting endorphins: Beltway journalists asking him questions as though he mattered.

Massie was first elected as a congressman from Kentucky in 2012 and will have warmed a seat there for more than a dozen years before he leaves. He could have actually worked on a particular issue and developed some valuable expertise. Instead, he became a kind of House moth, attracted to camera lights whenever they were turned his way.

HEGSETH RIPS IMPEACHMENT PUSH FROM OUTGOING REPUBLICAN AS 'FARCE,' 'STUNT'

Massie’s "accomplishments," if there are any genuine ones, are unknown to many beyond his own inner circle. He gets credit along with a handful of others for the provision in the 2018 Farm Bill that removed hemp from the federal controlled substances definition, opening the way for commercial production nationwide. That is it.

Massie got hooked on those cable channel lights of television, so he moved on from hemp and got hooked on the Epstein files. Massie rode that particular horse very hard, never taking his eyes off his own weird goal of getting the entire file dropped on the public. He deployed a discharge petition to get a vote and lured three other Republicans into joining him — Marjorie Taylor Greene of Georgia, Lauren Boebert of Colorado and Nancy Mace of South Carolina.

All four will be gone by Jan. 3. The result of the release of those files? A few folks got gored, like former British ambassador to the United States Lord Peter Mandelson and former U.K. Prime Minister Keir Starmer. But there was nothing in those voluminous files that implicated President Trump in Epstein’s crimes. Massie got zero out of that stunt except a precedent for breaking the long-established practice of not releasing raw files from investigations.

HUGH HEWITT: THREE BIG LEGAL FIGHTS ARE LOOMING, AND TRUMP NEEDS ANSWERS BEFORE JANUARY

Discharge petitions are a break with party leadership and rarely end well. New York Republican Rep. Mike Lawler forced a discharge petition on his own conference that required a vote on extending Obamacare subsidies. Three other Republicans joined Lawler in the stunt and only managed to embarrass his GOP colleagues who voted no on the actual bill. Brian Fitzpatrick, Rob Bresnahan and Ryan Mackenzie all joined Lawler on that petition. All four lost last week.

Stunts are remembered mostly by those they hurt. The enormity of the blue tsunami should not obscure the fact that all eight Republicans who turned on their caucus will be out on their backs come January, right along with many other members of the "Knucklehead Caucus" who kneecapped then-Speaker Kevin McCarthy in October 2023.

TRUMP CALLS OUT REP THOMAS MASSIE: 'KENTUCKY, GET THIS LOSER OUT OF POLITICS' TUESDAY

What all these rogue Republicans thought was "good politics" could not save them, and their demands for attention won’t be easily forgotten. Lobbying and public affairs firms are going to say "pass" if and when these types come looking for work. Which company wants to be represented by Massie et al.? If they would stab their own party, why would they stay loyal to their prospective new employers and clients?

Not that it matters to Democrats now. With their enormous majority, Democrats will call impeachment votes again and again, and they can count on near-unanimous support from their caucus.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

That means many hearings on many articles of impeachment, some of which will pass, and then hours, days, weeks and months of the Senate’s time will be spent on impeachment trials.

As with the idiotic demand from Massie for a vote on impeachment, so will it be with every impeachment proceeding in 2027-2028: lots of media attention for those who emerge as champions of the efforts to finally "get Trump."

They won’t succeed, of course. Even if they secured the necessary number of senators to vote for extended trials on every different impeachment article, enough GOP senators won’t vote for removal. It’s all a gigantic waste of time.

My unsolicited suggestion for President Trump: Get a list of Supreme Court law clerks from the past six years and interview those who are, in fact, (1) believers in Article II powers and (2) able to verbally battle with and best a White House press corps that will rival that of Nixon’s last two years in its collective combativeness.

President Trump is his own best defender, but a young, very smart, very articulate lawyer who knows the Constitution inside and out and doesn’t flinch from making arguments based on Article II powers is the ticket to at least getting his message out over the legacy media’s insatiable appetite for scandal and controversy as they gather their numbers for the last gasp in their 12-year war against Trump.
